core_principles: Bilateral squats are highly effective for quadriceps strengthening during the descending, holding, and ascending phases.
Varying stance width and foot position does not significantly alter quadriceps activation, though a wide stance can increase adductor longus and gluteus maximus activity.
Deep squats with maximal knee flexion may increase gluteus maximus activation during the ascending phase.
Maintaining proper knee alignment is critical, as frontal (medial) and sagittal (anterior) malalignment alters muscle activation patterns of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and calves.
common_mistakes: Medio-lateral (ML) malalignment (purposefully displacing the knee medially, similar to knee valgus).
Antero-posterior (AP) malalignment (purposefully displacing the knee anteriorly beyond control alignment).
Poorly performed squats that alter lower extremity alignment and gluteal activation.
specific_findings: The study evaluated twenty-eight healthy, uninjured subjects (19 women, 9 men, 21.5 +/- 3 years, 170 +/- 8.4 cm, 65.7 +/- 11.8 kg).
Vastus lateralis, medialis, and rectus femoris activity decreased in the medio-lateral (ML) malaligned squat compared with the control squat.

In the antero-posterior (AP) malaligned squat, vastus lateralis, medialis, and rectus femoris activity decreased during initial descent and final ascent, but vastus lateralis and rectus femoris activation increased during initial ascent compared with the control.
The biceps femoris and gastrocnemius displayed increased activation during both malaligned squats compared with the control squat.
Normalized EMG data (MVIC) represented the squat cycle with 50% representing peak knee flexion and 0 and 99% representing fully extended.

common_mistakes: Medial knee displacement (knees collapsing inward or medio-lateral malalignment).
Lifting heels off the floor during a squat (antero-posterior malalignment).

specific_findings: Control squats were performed to 90 degrees of flexion.

The medio-lateral (ML) malaligned squat resulted in significantly increased dorsiflexion, ankle inversion, knee flexion, knee abduction, and hip adduction during approximately 10-85% of the squat cycle compared with the control squat.

The squat cycle was defined as 100 points where 50% represents peak knee flexion, 0% and 99% represent full knee extension, 0-24% represents initial descent, 25-49% represents final descent, 50-74% represents initial ascent, and 75-99% represents final ascent.
Maximal voluntary isometric contractions (MVICs) for the vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, and biceps femoris were collected with knees flexed to 90 degrees.
MVICs for the lateral and medial gastrocnemius were collected with the subject lying prone and in 10 degrees of plantarflexion.

core_principles: Maintain proper medio-lateral (ML) and antero-posterior (AP) alignment during the squat to ensure optimal muscle recruitment.
Avoid malalignment to prevent significant decreases in quadriceps (vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and rectus femoris) activation during key phases of the squat.
Ensure proper hip flexion throughout the squat cycle (especially between 14-71% of the movement) to maintain correct biomechanics.
Prevent compensatory muscle activation patterns, such as over-activation of the biceps femoris and lateral gastrocnemius, which occur during malaligned squats.
common_mistakes: Medio-lateral (ML) malalignment during the squat cycle.
Antero-posterior (AP) malalignment during the squat cycle.
Decreased hip flexion during 14–71% of the squat cycle.
Allowing knee valgus or varus (ML malalignment) which reduces vastus medialis and vastus lateralis activation during the final ascent.
specific_findings: Participants demonstrated significantly decreased hip flexion during 14–71% of the squat cycle compared with the control squat.
Vastus lateralis had decreased activation during final ascent (96–99%) of the squat cycle in the ML malaligned squat with a very large effect size of 26.21.
Vastus medialis activation decreased during the final phase of ascent (92–98%) of the squat cycle in the ML malaligned squat with a very large effect size of 23.78.

Rectus femoris activation decreased during the initial (15–18%) and final phase of descent (28–48%) and final phase of ascent (85–99%) of the squat cycle in the ML malaligned squat (Effect sizes: 24.90, 21.72).
Biceps femoris activation increased during the initial phase of descent (11–21%) and beginning of the final phase of descent (25–28%) during the ML malaligned squat (Effect sizes: 4.71, 13.14).
Lateral gastrocnemius was more active during the ML malaligned squat in the initial (51–69%) and final phase of ascent (71–82%, 85–90%, 96–99%) (Effect sizes: 3.90, 11.53).
Medial gastrocnemius was less active during the initial (1–7%) phase of the squat cycle.

core_principles: Proper antero-posterior and mediolateral alignment during a squat is critical for balanced muscle recruitment.
Antero-posterior malalignment alters joint kinematics, specifically increasing anterior knee displacement and decreasing lateral knee displacement.
Maintaining proper ankle dorsiflexion and hip flexion is necessary to avoid compensatory muscle activation patterns in the quadriceps, hamstrings, and calves.
Malalignment can lead to over-reliance on the biceps femoris and gastrocnemius throughout the squat movement.
common_mistakes: Antero-posterior (AP) malalignment during the squat.
Mediolateral (ML) malalignment during the squat.
Insufficient ankle dorsiflexion during the squat cycle.
Excessive ankle inversion during the squat.
Decreased hip flexion and increased knee flexion (excessive forward knee travel) during the squat.
specific_findings: During the ascending phases of the ML malaligned squat, the medial gastrocnemius was more active at 65–69%, 75–78%, and 85–94% of the squat cycle compared with the control squat.
AP malaligned squats demonstrated significantly less dorsiflexion during 21–95% of the squat cycle.
The AP malaligned squat increased knee flexion from 22 to 80% of the squat cycle and decreased hip flexion from 5 to 77% of the squat cycle.
Ankle inversion increased from 10 to 92% of the AP malaligned squat compared with the control squat.
Participants demonstrated decreased knee adduction during 15–75% of the AP malaligned squat.
Vastus lateralis had decreased activation in the AP malaligned squat during initial descent (2–13%) and final ascent (87–99%), but increased activation during initial ascent (59–66%).
Vastus medialis activation decreased during initial (11–31%) and final descent (39–48%), as well as final ascent (81–98%) of the AP malaligned squat.
Rectus femoris activation decreased during initial descent (8–21%) and final ascent (82–99%), but increased during initial ascent (52–71%) in the AP malaligned squat.
The biceps femoris had increased activation in all 4 phases of the AP malaligned squat (effect size range = 1.66, 7.94).
The lateral gastrocnemius activation increased during the AP malaligned squat during all phases of descent and ascent (1–95%).

Anteroposterior (AP) malalignment during the descent and ascent phases.
